title: Challenger Astronauts Memorialized on the Moon
description: Apollo is a 524 km-wide impact basin located inside the giant South Pole–Aitken basin on the Moon. NASA identified it as a potential region for future human lunar exploration. After the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster, seven craters on Apollo Basin's eastern rim were named in honor of the seven crew members who lost their lives.

title: Apollo 8’s Iconic Earthrise
description: The Apollo 8 crew captured a rising Earth about five degrees above the Moon’s horizon near 110° east longitude. Taken on December 24 at 15:40 GMT, the image shows Earth's sunset line crossing Africa, the South Pole near its left end, and clouds covering North and South America.

title: A New View of the Moon
description: On April 6, 2026, the Artemis II crew captured Earth setting behind the Moon’s curved edge. The image shows the Orientale and Hertzsprung impact basins, Vavilov crater, and secondary crater chains. The dark side of Earth is experiencing nighttime, while clouds are visible over Australia and Oceania.

title: Faces of Shackleton
description: Shackleton Crater is a 21 km-wide crater at the Moon's south pole, where most of its interior remains permanently in shadow. The image shows four views of the crater: its topography from LOLA, visible lighting conditions from SMART-1, illumination patterns from the LRO Camera, and radar data from Mini-RF overlaid on a shaded relief map.

title: Wrinkle Ridge in Mare Crisium
description: Mare Crisium is a large, dark, basaltic plain on the Moon. Basaltic plains on the Moon were created by early volcanic eruptions. Mare Crisium was once flooded with basaltic lava, a dark, runny lava commonly found on Earth.

title: Total lunar eclipse
description: During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon enters Earth's inner shadow (umbra). Sunlight passing through Earth's atmosphere reaches the Moon, making it appear reddish or orange. This happens because blue and violet light scatter more easily, while red and orange light pass through. More dust or clouds in Earth's atmosphere can make the Moon appear even redder.
